title: Choosing an engine: DuckDB, Spark, Trino and friends
goal: By the end, you can size a query by the bytes it really reads and decide with numbers whether it needs one machine or a cluster, explain why DuckDB beats Spark on one laptop and where that flips, say what Polars, pandas, DataFusion, Trino, ClickHouse and Flink are for, and sketch the whole design for a payments company.
opening:
Picture a team asked for a monthly report on three years of card payments. The table holds 4 TB, four million million bytes. "Four terabytes," someone says, "so we need a cluster," a group of machines that share the work. Now, every morning, twenty machines start up, plan, hand out tasks and pass data around, to answer a question a laptop answers in three seconds.

It's easy to size the tool by the table. The table's size is the one number everybody knows, and big feels like it needs big. But a query rarely reads the whole table.

What batch output is for: ETL, ML features and serving data followed the night's results to the people and programs that read them. Which engine, the program that reads the data and works out answers, should do each job? In this lesson, we'll size a query by the bytes it really reads, race DuckDB against Spark on one laptop, place the other engines, and sketch the whole design. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A payments table holds 4 TB of Parquet, a file format that stores each column apart. It covers 3 years, with each day's payments in their own folder, a partition, and it has 60 columns of similar size. The finance report reads 4 columns for the last 30 days. Roughly how many bytes does it read?
options: 4 TB: a query reads the whole table
About 110 GB: the last 30 days
About 7 GB: 30 of 1,095 days, and 4 of 60 columns
Almost nothing: the answer is saved from last time
warmup.why: Skipping the other partitions keeps 30 of 1,095 days: 110 GB. Parquet keeps each column apart, so reading 4 of 60 columns leaves about 7.3 GB. That number, not the 4 TB, decides the engine, and at a few GB a second it's seconds on one machine. The second option is the trap: it skips the days but forgets the columns, which Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown showed are stored apart.

sections.h: Sizing a query by the bytes it reads, not by the size of the table
sections.body:
This last lesson turns the track's numbers into one decision: which engine should run a given piece of work? DuckDB, Spark and Trino are all engines. "The payments table is 4 TB, so we need Spark" sizes the wrong thing. The first lesson of this track, Why big data systems exist, and when you don't need one, gave the formula that answers it. A scan costs the bytes it reads, divided by the speed of its slowest stage. The lessons on Hive, Parquet and Iceberg then showed how much a good layout shrinks "the bytes it reads". Put the two together, and you get a method you can run before you pick an engine. The stepper walks it for one query, then for two others on the same table.

Step 1, skip partitions. A partition is one slice of a table, here one day's payments, stored apart. Count only the partitions the filter can match. A report on the last 30 days of a table split by day reads 30 of 1,095 days: 110 GB of the 4 TB.

Step 2, skip columns. Parquet, the file format this track keeps tables in, stores each column apart, so count only the columns the query uses. 4 of 60 columns of similar size: 7.3 GB.

Step 3, divide by one machine's scan speed. That's the slower of two numbers. One is the cores decoding Parquet, turning its packed bytes back into values: the number of cores times the speed of each. The other is the storage feeding them. On a laptop, that's its fast built-in disk, an NVMe drive. On a cloud machine (a VM, a slice of a big computer that you rent), it's the network link to object storage. That's a service such as Amazon S3 that keeps files for you over the network. The Try it measures your laptop. While busy with other jobs, this one decoded 300 to 360 MB/s on one core and about 2 GB/s on all 12. A big cloud machine reading S3 gets about 1.5 GB/s. If several people run the query at once, they share that speed. 7.3 GB at 3 GB/s is about 2.4 seconds.

Step 4, check memory. The **working set** is what the query must hold at once. For a join, that's a hash table (a lookup structure in memory) built from one side. For a total per group, it's one running total per group. For the report it's a few MB. For a join of two years of payments against two years of chargebacks (payments the bank took back), it can be hundreds of GB. DuckDB can spill to disk when memory runs out, writing what doesn't fit to temporary files, at a cost. So treat memory as the comfortable limit.

Then route. Moving goods works the same way. Most days a company sends an envelope, and a courier on a bike beats any truck: no loading dock, no schedule, door to door in minutes. That's one machine. If one machine meets the time budget and holds the working set, use it: DuckDB on a laptop, or on one cloud machine next to the data. If not, use a cluster, sized to the larger of the two needs.

Forty offices that each want a box by noon need a fleet of vans that leave at once: an engine that answers fast for many users, such as Trino. Moving a whole archive to a new building needs lorries with a plan for a breakdown on the way: an engine that retries failed tasks, such as Spark. And mail that never stops needs a postal round. That's a streaming engine, for work that never ends, like the fraud counts of Streaming in Spark: Structured Streaming and watermarks.

**Size the query, not the table. Then let the numbers pick the engine.**

The lab turns these rules into code. Next, we'll test the first route by racing the bike against a lorry on one laptop.

try.title: Measure your laptop, then size five workloads
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `LaptopNumbersDemo`. It writes 10 million payments as Parquet with DuckDB and times a two-column total on 1 thread and on all cores. Then it works out five workloads on a 4 TB payments table: the bytes each reads, and the seconds on your laptop and on a cloud machine that reads object storage at 1.5 GB/s.
Before you read the table, guess which of the five need more than one machine.

Your numbers depend on your processor, on what else is running, and on the page cache, the operating system's copy of recently used files in memory. The files were just written, so they're in memory. From a cold disk or from S3, the storage stage sets the speed instead.

code.title: LaptopNumbersDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l15.demo

import com.sun.management.OperatingSystemMXBean
import java.io.File
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory

/**
 * Measures the two numbers the engine rubric needs from this laptop: how fast DuckDB decodes
 * Parquet on one core and on all of them. Then works out, for five workloads of a payments
 * company, the bytes each reads after pruning and the seconds it would take here and on a
 * 64-core cloud VM that reads object storage at 1.5 GB/s.
 */
fun main() {
    freshDemoDir()
    val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()
    val memory = (ManagementFactory.getOperatingSystemMXBean() as OperatingSystemMXBean).totalMemorySize
    println("this machine: $cores cores, %.0f GiB of memory".format(memory / (1L shl 30).toDouble()))

    val c = duck()
    val payments = File(DEMO_DIR, "payments")
    writePayments(c, 10_000_000, payments, File(DEMO_DIR, "merchants"))
    val glob = "${payments.absolutePath}/*.parquet"
    // the compressed bytes of the two columns the query needs, from the Parquet footers (lesson 5)
    val bytes = (c.rows("SELECT sum(total_compressed_size) FROM parquet_metadata('$glob') " +
        "WHERE path_in_schema IN ('amount_cents', 'status')").first()[0] as Number).toLong()
    val query = "SELECT status, sum(amount_cents) FROM read_parquet('$glob') GROUP BY status"
    fun bestMillis(threads: Int): Double {
        c.run("SET threads = $threads")
        return (1..5).minOf {
            val t0 = System.nanoTime()
            c.rows(query)
            (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6
        }
    }
    val one = bestMillis(1)
    val all = bestMillis(cores)
    val perCore = bytes / (one / 1000)
    val allCores = bytes / (all / 1000)
    println("DuckDB, sum by status over 10,000,000 payments (2 columns, %.0f MB compressed, files in the page cache):".format(bytes / 1e6))
    println("   1 thread:  %5.0f ms, so about %.0f MB/s per core".format(one, perCore / 1e6))
    println("  %2d threads: %5.0f ms, so about %.1f GB/s".format(cores, all, allCores / 1e9))

    // four TB of payments over 3 years (1,095 days), 60 columns of similar size
    data class W(val name: String, val days: Int, val columns: Int, val users: Int)
    val workloads = listOf(
        W("monthly finance report", 30, 4, 1),
        W("one merchant's disputes, ad hoc", 365, 6, 1),
        W("merchant dashboard, 40 users", 90, 4, 40),
        W("nightly settlement over a week", 7, 12, 1),
        W("fraud feature backfill, 3 years", 1095, 30, 1),
    )
    val vm = 1.5e9
    println("%-34s %10s %12s %12s".format("workload (4 TB table)", "reads", "this laptop", "cloud VM"))
    for (w in workloads) {
        val read = 4e12 * w.days / 1095 * w.columns / 60
        println("%-34s %7.1f GB %10.1f s %10.1f s".format(w.name, read / 1e9, read / allCores * w.users, read / vm * w.users))
    }
    c.close()
}

sections.h: One laptop, one question: DuckDB against Spark
sections.body:
Here's the first route, measured. Ten million payments sit in 106 MB of Parquet, in 8 files. The question: per day and per kind of shop (its merchant category, `mcc`, such as cafés or bookshops), how many captured payments were there, and how much money? A captured payment is one where the money has really moved. It's a filter, a join to a table of 500 shops, and a group-by.

DuckDB answered in 50 to 180 ms. Spark ran in local mode, all of Spark in one program, on the same 12 cores. It took about 1.4 seconds on its best of three runs, and 8 to 10 seconds on its first. Starting its session took another 3 to 4 seconds. Both returned the same 140 rows. Across runs on this busy laptop, Spark's best was 10 to 30 times DuckDB's best. The gap comes from what Spark is built for.

Look at what each engine does for that query. DuckDB is a library: it runs inside your own program, in the same process (a running program and its memory). It reads the Parquet column chunks it needs and decodes them into vectors, batches of a couple of thousand values. Then it runs the filter, the hash join (matching rows through a hash table) and the totals over those vectors in compiled C++ code. All its threads, lines of work running at once, share one hash table in memory. Nothing leaves the process.

Spark does what The Spark execution model and the two lessons after it described, because it's built for many machines. The driver, its main program, parses and optimizes the plan. It cuts the plan into stages around the shuffle, the step that moves rows between tasks so that rows with the same key meet. Then it schedules the tasks on executors, worker programs on each machine. Each task reads its slice of the files, builds partial totals, and writes shuffle files for the next stage to fetch, even when the "network" is the same laptop. The rows pass through the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code, with fresh code generated for each query and memory cleaned up as it goes.

Each of those costs buys something on a cluster: tasks that can be retried on another machine, shuffles spread over hundreds of disks, and executors that survive a lost machine. On one machine they buy nothing, and they're paid on every query. It's hiring a lorry, a crew and a route plan to carry one envelope across town.

The fair summary: fixed costs per query decide small queries, and the combined speed of many machines decides big ones. Somewhere in between is a crossover. There, one machine can't scan the bytes in time, and Spark's costs become a small tax on a job that couldn't run anywhere else. For this laptop, at 2 GB/s with a budget of a few minutes, that point is a few hundred GB read. Or it's a working set bigger than its 32 GiB of memory.

Spark is closing the gap from its side. Spark 4.3 added an opt-in setting, `spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled`, that runs small queries as one task with no shuffle. And native engines such as Apache Gluten with Velox replace the JVM's row-by-row work with C++ that processes whole vectors.

DuckDB isn't alone on one machine. DuckDB 2.0 (October 2026, a release with long-term support) added faster reads of Parquet on object storage and a client-server protocol, so one running DuckDB can serve a small team. Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust, a fast programming language. (A DataFrame is a table you work with from code, through calls such as filter, join and group.) Its lazy interface plans the whole query before running it, like Spark. Since 2.0 (October 2026; 2.1 is current), it spills to disk by default once a query needs more than 80% of memory.

pandas (3.1 is current) runs each call at once, one step at a time, in memory. Version 3.0 made copy-on-write the default, so changing a copy no longer changes the original. It also gave strings their own type. Both change how old notebooks (pages of code and results) behave. Apache DataFusion is a query engine library in Rust that other engines are built from, Spark's native accelerator Comet among them. The method is the same for all of them: if the working set fits one machine, a one-machine engine wins on overhead. Next, the routes that do need a cluster, and how several engines share one table.

try.title: One question, two engines
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `SameQueryDemo`. It writes 10 million payments and 500 shops as Parquet with DuckDB. Then it runs the same filter, join and totals three times in DuckDB and three times in Spark (`local[*]`, every core), and checks that the answers match.
Before it runs, predict the ratio of Spark's best time to DuckDB's best.

Why is Spark's first run so much slower than its third? Think of the planning The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching said Spark does at the start of every query, and of what the JVM does the first time it runs code.

code.title: SameQueryDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l15.demo

import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.count
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum
import java.io.File

/**
 * Ten million payments as Parquet, and one question asked of two engines on this laptop: per day
 * and merchant category, how many captured payments and how much money? Times DuckDB and Spark
 * (local[*], every core) and checks that the answers match.
 */
fun main() {
    freshDemoDir()
    val payments = File(DEMO_DIR, "payments")
    val merchants = File(DEMO_DIR, "merchants")
    val c = duck()
    writePayments(c, 10_000_000, payments, merchants)
    println("payments: 10,000,000 rows in ${payments.list()!!.size} Parquet files, %.0f MB".format(megabytes(payments)))

    fun timed(runs: Int, block: () -> List<List<Any?>>): Pair<List<List<Any?>>, List<Long>> {
        var result: List<List<Any?>> = emptyList()
        val times = (1..runs).map {
            val t0 = System.nanoTime()
            result = block()
            (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000
        }
        return result to times
    }

    val (duckAnswer, duckTimes) = timed(3) {
        c.rows("""
            SELECT p.dt::VARCHAR, m.mcc, count(*), sum(p.amount_cents)
            FROM read_parquet('${payments.absolutePath}/*.parquet') p
            JOIN read_parquet('${merchants.absolutePath}/*.parquet') m ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
            WHERE p.status = 'CAPTURED'
            GROUP BY ALL
            ORDER BY 1, 2""")
    }
    println("DuckDB: ${duckTimes.joinToString(", ") { "$it ms" }}")

    val t0 = System.nanoTime()
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val startup = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000
    val (sparkAnswer, sparkTimes) = timed(3) {
        spark.read().parquet(payments.absolutePath).where(col("status").equalTo(lit("CAPTURED")))
            .join(spark.read().parquet(merchants.absolutePath), "merchant_id")
            .groupBy(col("dt").cast("string").alias("day"), col("mcc"))
            .agg(count(lit(1)), sum("amount_cents"))
            .orderBy("day", "mcc")
            .collectAsList()
            .map { r -> (0 until 4).map { r.get(it) } }
    }
    println("Spark:  ${sparkTimes.joinToString(", ") { "$it ms" }} (plus $startup ms to start the session)")

    val same = duckAnswer.map { it.map(Any?::toString) } == sparkAnswer.map { it.map(Any?::toString) }
    println("answers: ${duckAnswer.size} rows each, identical: $same")
    println("first row: ${duckAnswer.first()}")
    println("best run, Spark / DuckDB: about %.0fx".format(sparkTimes.min().toDouble() / duckTimes.min()))
    spark.stop()
    c.close()
}

sections.h: The other routes: Trino, ClickHouse and Flink over one shared table
sections.body:
The method has two more routes, and both point at engines this track didn't run: Trino, and a streaming engine. ClickHouse sits off to the side. What makes them usable together is the work of Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg and Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs. The table lives once, in Iceberg, a set of rules for keeping a table as plain files and changing it one commit at a time. It sits behind a catalog, the service that holds each table's pointer. Any engine that speaks Iceberg reads the same files. The Try it shows the smallest case. Spark writes a table, and DuckDB reads it through Iceberg's metadata, the files that list the table's data files, without copying anything. Then DuckDB sees Spark's next commit as a new snapshot, a saved version of the table.

Here the moving picture breaks, in a good way. Goods sit in one place, and one vehicle takes them. Data can be read by all the engines at once: the bike, the vans and the lorries pick up from the same shelf, and nothing needs moving first.

Trino is a distributed SQL engine, one that splits each query over many machines. A coordinator plans each query, and workers run its stages in parallel. They pass data between stages in memory as it flows, with no shuffle files like Spark's. That makes Trino fast to answer: on a big enough cluster, a query over tens of GB returns in seconds, and many users can share the cluster. The trade is that a failed worker fails its queries by default. Trino has a fault-tolerant mode (`retry-policy=TASK`) that saves the data between stages, at a cost.

Trino reads Iceberg through a REST catalog, a catalog you talk to over the web, with a few lines of settings: `connector.name=iceberg`, `iceberg.catalog.type=rest`, and the catalog's address. Through other connectors, it can join those tables with PostgreSQL (a popular database), Kafka (a program that keeps logs of messages) or other sources. Trino 484 is current and needs Java 25. Use it as the shared SQL engine for analysts and BI tools (business intelligence: programs that draw charts and dashboards from SQL). That's the dashboard route.

ClickHouse is a database server that stores data by column, in its own storage, called MergeTree. MergeTree sorts data on disk by a key you choose and merges small pieces in the background. ClickHouse is built for answers in well under a second over fresh event data, such as a dashboard where shops watch the last minute of payments. It can read Kafka topics directly and query Iceberg tables, but it shines on data it owns, so it adds a second copy of the data. Use it when "seconds" isn't fast enough.

Flink, from the Stream processing track, is the engine for streaming as the main product: large state kept per key, and a reaction to each event as it arrives. Spark's real-time mode, from Streaming in Spark, is narrowing the gap for simpler pipelines.

The pattern: the lakehouse turned "which engine stores our data?" into "which engine runs this work?", and that's the question the method answers. Next, we'll put the answers together for the whole payments company.

try.title: One Iceberg table, two engines
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `TwoEnginesOneTableDemo`. Spark creates an Iceberg table in a Hadoop catalog (a catalog kept as a folder) and inserts a million payments. DuckDB then answers the same question with `iceberg_scan` on the table's folder. Spark appends 500,000 more, and both answer again. DuckDB downloads its Iceberg extension the first time, so this demo needs the internet once.
Predict what DuckDB's `iceberg_snapshots` shows before and after the second append.
DuckDB never talked to Spark. What did it read to find the table's files?

code.title: TwoEnginesOneTableDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l15.demo

import java.io.File

/**
 * One Iceberg table, two engines. Spark creates and appends to the table; DuckDB reads the same
 * files through Iceberg's metadata, with no copy and no Spark. Then Spark appends again and DuckDB
 * sees the new snapshot. DuckDB's Iceberg extension is downloaded once on first use.
 */
fun main() {
    freshDemoDir()
    val spark = demoSpark()
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.payments (payment_id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, status STRING, amount_cents BIGINT, " +
        "created_at TIMESTAMP) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))")
    fun append(from: Long, n: Long) = spark.sql("""
        INSERT INTO lake.pay.payments
        SELECT id, CAST(pmod(hash(id), 500) AS INT), CASE WHEN id % 5 = 0 THEN 'REFUNDED' ELSE 'CAPTURED' END,
               CAST(pmod(hash(id, 2), 250000) + 100 AS BIGINT),
               timestamp_seconds(1793491200 + (id % 3) * 86400 + pmod(hash(id, 4), 86400))
        FROM range($from, ${from + n})""")
    append(0, 1_000_000)
    val table = File(DEMO_DIR, "warehouse/pay/payments").absolutePath
    val question = "SELECT count(*) AS payments, sum(amount_cents) AS amount FROM %s WHERE status = 'CAPTURED'"

    fun sparkSays() = spark.sql(question.format("lake.pay.payments")).first().let { "${it.getLong(0)} payments, ${it.getLong(1)} cents" }
    println("Spark reads:  ${sparkSays()}")
    duck().use { c ->
        c.run("INSTALL iceberg")
        c.run("LOAD iceberg")
        fun duckSays() = c.rows(question.format("iceberg_scan('$table')")).first().let { "${it[0]} payments, ${it[1]} cents" }
        println("DuckDB reads: ${duckSays()}")
        println("DuckDB sees snapshots: " + c.rows("SELECT sequence_number, snapshot_id FROM iceberg_snapshots('$table') ORDER BY 1").map { it[0] })

        append(1_000_000, 500_000)
        println("after Spark appends 500,000 more:")
        println("Spark reads:  ${sparkSays()}")
        println("DuckDB reads: ${duckSays()}")
        println("DuckDB sees snapshots: " + c.rows("SELECT sequence_number, snapshot_id FROM iceberg_snapshots('$table') ORDER BY 1").map { it[0] })
    }
    spark.stop()
}

sections.h: Most questions are small, some jobs aren't: the whole payments lakehouse
sections.body:
Jordan Tigani's essay "Big Data is Dead", which the first lesson of this track quoted, argues that most companies never had big data. Most customers of BigQuery, Google's cloud warehouse (a database built for questions over history), stored under 1 TB, and 90% of queries processed under 100 MB. It's worth taking seriously, and worth reading critically. Tigani was a founding engineer of BigQuery and now runs MotherDuck, which sells DuckDB in the cloud, so the conclusion also suits his business. His numbers come from one product, and he calls them approximate. And they describe queries, not jobs. Think of the import that writes a few TB a day. Or the backfill that works out three years of fraud features again, the numbers about each card that a fraud model reads. Or a join of two years of payments against two years of disputes. Those are the 1% that still need a cluster, and every payments company has a few.

DuckDB's own test in March 2026 pushed the point to the extreme. A $700 MacBook with 8 GB of memory ran ClickBench, a standard set of 43 test queries, over 100 million rows (14 GB of Parquet). From a cold start, it took 59.7 seconds. A 16-core cloud machine took 145.1 seconds, and a 192-core one 169.7, because the cloud machines read from disks across the network. Once the data was in memory, the 192-core machine won, 4.35 seconds to 54.3. The laptop also ran TPC-DS, a much heavier standard test, at scale factor 100 (roughly 100 GB of data) in 15.5 minutes. At scale factor 300, it took 79 minutes and spilled up to 80 GB to disk.

Both sides are right about different work, which is the method's point. Run it per workload, and the payments company of this track ends up with the design in the figure.

Every payment goes into Kafka, a program that keeps an ordered log of messages that any program can read again. Change data capture, a program that copies every change from the main database into the log, adds the corrections. A Spark Structured Streaming job, Spark's way of running a job that never ends, appends them all to Iceberg tables every minute. It does so exactly once, so a crash never loses or doubles a payment (the Stream processing track). The tables live as Parquet on object storage. A REST catalog such as Apache Polaris, a free one, holds their pointers and access rules (Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs).

Spark batch runs the heavy jobs: the nightly settlement, the sums of what each shop is owed, over the week's corrections, plus backfills and model features. Trino serves analysts and BI tools that share the same tables. Finance and engineers answer one-off questions with DuckDB on a laptop or one cloud machine. If shops need a dashboard faster than a second, a ClickHouse copy of recent events is added, and nothing else changes.

Something must run the jobs in order and keep the tables healthy: the orchestrator of Orchestrating batch work. An Airflow 3 DAG, a chain of jobs that wait for each other, is scheduled on the payments asset, Airflow's name for the payments table. It runs when the day lands. It compacts yesterday's partitions (merges their small files) and expires old snapshots (Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs), then runs settlement, then refreshes the reports. Every task is keyed to its day, so retries and backfills are safe. Scores and limits that the live app reads go back through the build-and-swap of What batch output is for.

Start small and let the numbers move you. A team with 300 GB of payments can run this whole picture with Iceberg on object storage, a REST catalog and DuckDB. It adds Spark on the day the method says a job no longer fits one machine.

The method has limits. It says nothing about cost, about the work of running each extra engine, or about many writers on one table; Go deeper covers them. And look at the figure once more: everything starts from one log, and every table, report and score is a copy worked out from it. Keeping all those copies right as the business changes is the next track's subject.

mistake: The common mistake is choosing the engine by the size of the data at rest, or by what the last company used. "The payments table is 4 TB" gets a Spark cluster, and then every report pays seconds of scheduling, shuffle files and JVM work to read 7 GB. Or the reverse: a laptop DuckDB setup is pushed to run the three-year backfill whose join needs 600 GB, and it never finishes. It happens because table size is the number everyone knows, while the bytes a query reads after skipping days and columns take a minute of arithmetic. The fix is that minute. For each important piece of work, write down the partitions read, the columns read, the slowest stage's speed, the working set, the number of people running it at once and the time budget, and route each one on its own. Keep the data in one open table format, so each piece of work can move engines when its numbers change.

compare.title: The same question in DuckDB's SQL and in Spark's DataFrame code

a.label: DuckDB
a.title: inside your program, reading Parquet where it lies
a.src:
SELECT p.dt, m.mcc, count(*) AS payments,
       sum(p.amount_cents) AS amount_cents
FROM read_parquet('payments/*.parquet') p
JOIN read_parquet('merchants/*.parquet') m
  ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
WHERE p.status = 'CAPTURED'
GROUP BY p.dt, m.mcc
ORDER BY p.dt, m.mcc;

b.label: Spark
b.title: a driver, stages and tasks, even in local mode

compare.note: The plan is the same: read two sets of Parquet files, filter, join on `merchant_id` with a hash table built from the small side, total, sort. The difference is everything around it. DuckDB runs the plan inside your program, with all threads sharing one hash table. Spark plans stages, sends the shops table to every executor, writes shuffle files for the totals, schedules a task per slice of the files and collects the result back to the driver. Those steps let Spark grow past one machine and survive failures. On one machine, they're overhead you pay on every query.

steps.say: Write down the machines you can use: a laptop with a fast local disk, and the standard cloud machine (VM) that reads object storage.
steps.code:
val laptop = Machine(cores = 10, memoryBytes = 16 * GB, decodeBytesPerSecondPerCore = 500 * MB, ioBytesPerSecond = 3 * GB)
val vm = Machine(cores = 64, memoryBytes = 256 * GB, decodeBytesPerSecondPerCore = 500 * MB, ioBytesPerSecond = 1_500 * MB)

steps.say: Describe each piece of work by what it reads and needs, not by the table. The finance report reads 4 of 60 columns for 30 of 1,095 days.
steps.code:
val report = Workload("monthly finance report", tableBytes = 4 * TB,
    partitionsRead = 30.0 / 1095, columnsRead = 4.0 / 60,
    workingSetBytes = 2 * GB, timeBudgetSeconds = 60.0)
EngineChoice.choose(report, laptop)
// Route(engine=SINGLE_NODE, bytesRead=7305936073, singleNodeSeconds=2.43, machines=1)

steps.say: The dashboard reads 22 GB, but 40 people run it at once with a 30-second budget, so they share one VM's scan speed. The method sends it to an interactive cluster.
steps.code:
val dashboard = report.copy(name = "merchant dashboard", partitionsRead = 90.0 / 1095,
    timeBudgetSeconds = 30.0, concurrent = 40)
EngineChoice.choose(dashboard, vm)
// 21.9 GB x 40 / 1.5 GB/s = 584 s on one VM -> INTERACTIVE_CLUSTER with ceil(584 / 30) = 20 machines

steps.say: The backfill's scan fits a 2-hour budget on one VM, but its join must hold 600 GB at once. Memory, not time, sizes the cluster, and a job that runs for hours needs task retries: a batch cluster.
steps.code:
val backfill = Workload("fraud feature backfill", tableBytes = 4 * TB, partitionsRead = 1.0,
    columnsRead = 0.5, workingSetBytes = 600 * GB, timeBudgetSeconds = 2 * 3600.0)
EngineChoice.choose(backfill, vm)
// 2 TB / 1.5 GB/s = 1,333 s (fits), 600 GB / 256 GB -> BATCH_CLUSTER with 3 machines

drill.title: Size a query in four lines
drill.prompt: From memory, size this query and route it. A 9 TB table of card payments covers 2 years (730 daily partitions) and has 45 columns of similar size. A fraud analyst wants 3 columns for the last 14 days, within 30 seconds, alone. Her laptop scans at 2 GB/s and has 32 GB of memory, and the working set is small. Then: what if 25 analysts run it at the same moment on one cloud machine at 1.5 GB/s?

answer.src:
partitions: 9 TB x 14 / 730          = 173 GB
columns:    173 GB x 3 / 45           = 11.5 GB
time:       11.5 GB / 2 GB/s          = 5.8 s   (budget 30 s)
memory:     small                     -> one machine: DuckDB on her laptop

25 analysts on one VM at 1.5 GB/s:
            11.5 GB x 25 / 1.5 GB/s   = 192 s   (budget 30 s)
            ceil(192 / 30)            = 7 machines -> an interactive cluster: Trino

recap: Size a query, not a table: bytes read = table bytes x share of partitions read x share of columns read. A 4 TB table often answers from a few GB.
Time on one machine = bytes read / the slower of (cores x decode speed) and storage speed, times the number of people sharing it. Check the working set against memory too.

If one machine meets the budget and holds the working set, use one machine (DuckDB). Otherwise size a cluster by the larger of time and memory: Trino for SQL that must answer in seconds for many people, Spark for long batch jobs that need task retries, a streaming engine for work that never ends.

On one laptop, DuckDB answers small queries 10 to 30 times faster than Spark in local mode, because Spark pays for scheduling, shuffle files and the JVM on every query. On a cluster, those costs buy growth and survival of failures.

Iceberg and a REST catalog let each piece of work pick its engine: Spark, Trino, DuckDB, Flink and ClickHouse can read the same tables without copies. The design for a payments company: Kafka, a streaming load into Iceberg, a REST catalog, Spark for heavy batch, Trino for shared SQL, DuckDB for one-off questions, and Airflow 3 assets running upkeep and reports when tables change.
The limit: the method counts bytes and seconds, not money, the work of running each extra engine, or many writers on one table, so check those before adding an engine.
closing:
We started with a team that bought twenty machines for a 4 TB table, when the report read 7 GB and a laptop answered in seconds. The bytes a query reads after skipping days and columns take a minute of arithmetic, and they decide.

Pick a question about data you know, such as last month's spending in your bank's export. Write down the rows and columns it really needs, and work out its size before you reach for a tool.

That ends the Batch processing and analytics track. Next, in Derived data and doing right, we'll trace every copy of a payment back to one record. How do you change a month of worked-out numbers without anyone seeing a gap?

quiz.q: A 6 TB payments table covers 2 years (730 daily partitions), with 50 columns of similar size. A report reads 5 columns of the last 7 days. One laptop scans at 2 GB/s. Roughly how long does the scan take?
options: About 50 minutes: 6 TB at 2 GB/s
About 30 seconds: one week of the table
About 3 seconds: 5.8 GB at 2 GB/s
Less than a millisecond, because Parquet has an index
quiz.why: 6 TB x 7 / 730 is 57.5 GB for a week. Times 5 / 50 for the columns, that's 5.8 GB, and at 2 GB/s about 3 seconds. The 50 minutes ignores skipping altogether; the 30 seconds skips days but reads all 50 columns. Parquet's statistics let an engine skip blocks of rows, but nothing turns a scan of 5.8 GB into a single lookup.

quiz.q: Thirty analysts open the same dashboard at 9:00. Each query reads 10 GB, and the budget is 20 seconds. One cloud machine scans 1.5 GB/s. What does the method say?
options: One machine: each query takes under 7 seconds
A Spark batch cluster, because there are many users
A streaming engine, because the dashboard refreshes
An interactive cluster of about 10 machines, because 30 queries share the machine's speed: 200 s of scanning against a 20 s budget
quiz.why: One query alone takes 10 / 1.5 = 6.7 s, but 30 at once share the machine: 200 s. 200 / 20 is 10 machines, and an answer in seconds for many people is Trino's job. The first option is the trap: it times one query as if nobody else were running. Spark's costs per query suit long batch jobs, and a dashboard that people refresh isn't a stream.

quiz.q: On a laptop, the same join and totals over 10 million rows take about 0.1 s in DuckDB and 1.4 s in Spark's local mode. What's the best explanation?
options: Spark reads the Parquet files row by row
DuckDB saves query results and hands them out again
Spark pays for planning stages, scheduling tasks, writing and fetching shuffle files and running in the JVM; on one machine those buy nothing
DuckDB skips the join because the shops table is small
quiz.why: Spark reads Parquet by column too, and both engines really run the join. Spark's fixed costs (the driver, stages split at the shuffle, tasks, shuffle files even on one laptop, code generated in the JVM) exist so that work can spread over machines and survive failures. On one machine they're pure overhead; on 100 machines reading terabytes they're a small tax. DuckDB's three runs didn't return a saved answer: each one read the files again.

quiz.q: Which statement about Trino, ClickHouse and Flink is right?
options: ClickHouse keeps data in its own MergeTree storage for answers in well under a second on fresh events; Trino queries data where it lives, such as Iceberg tables through a REST catalog
Trino stores tables in its own format, so data must be loaded into it first
Flink is a batch SQL engine for dashboards
All three need HDFS
quiz.why: Trino has no storage of its own; it reads through connectors, Iceberg with a REST catalog among them. ClickHouse is a database server that owns its storage, which is what makes it so fast on recent events, at the price of a second copy. Flink is a streaming-first engine for work that never stops and keeps state. None of them needs HDFS, Hadoop's file system; object storage is the usual home.

quiz.q: From Why big data systems exist, and when you don't need one: a team says "our payments table is 4 TB, we need a cluster". Its reports read 4 of 60 columns for the last 30 days of 3 years. What does that lesson's formula say first?
options: Yes: 4 TB at 500 MB/s is over 2 hours
Work out the bytes the query reads after skipping partitions and columns (about 7 GB), then divide by the slowest stage's speed: seconds on one machine
Use more machines until the time is under a minute
The answer depends only on the number of rows
quiz.why: That lesson's two levers were "more readers" and "fewer bytes", and it said to pull the fewer-bytes lever first. 4 TB x 30 / 1,095 x 4 / 60 is about 7.3 GB, a few seconds at a few GB/s. Sizing by the table's bytes at rest is exactly the mistake that lesson warned about.

flashcards.front: How do you size a query before choosing an engine?
flashcards.back: Bytes read = table bytes x share of partitions read x share of column bytes read. Then divide by one machine's scan speed.

flashcards.front: What sets one machine's scan speed?
flashcards.back: The slower of all its cores decoding (cores x speed per core) and the storage feeding them (a local disk, or the network to object storage).

flashcards.front: When does a query belong on one machine?
flashcards.back: When one machine meets the time budget, with everyone running it at once sharing that machine, and holds the working set in memory.

flashcards.front: Trino or Spark for a cluster?
flashcards.back: Trino for SQL that must answer in seconds for many people. Spark for long batch jobs that need task retries and big shuffles.

flashcards.front: Why is Spark slower than DuckDB on a laptop?
flashcards.back: Spark pays for the driver, planning stages, scheduling tasks, shuffle files and the JVM on every query. On one machine, those buy nothing.

flashcards.front: What does ClickHouse add that Trino doesn't?
flashcards.back: Its own storage (MergeTree), sorted and merged in the background, for answers in well under a second on fresh events, at the cost of a second copy.

terms.plain: The program that reads the data and works out the answer to a query, such as DuckDB, Spark or Trino.
The bytes a query must really scan after skipping partitions and columns.
How many bytes a second one machine can read and decode: the slower of its processor and its storage.
The data a query must hold in memory at once, such as a join's hash table or the running totals of a group-by.
An engine that runs a query inside one program on one machine, such as DuckDB.
Massively parallel processing: an engine like Trino that splits each query over many workers and passes data between them as it flows.
The query size where a cluster's combined speed starts to outweigh its own fixed costs per query.
A named piece of data that tasks declare they update, and whose changes can start other DAGs.

explain_back.prompt: Your director asks why the data platform plan uses DuckDB, Trino and Spark instead of "one engine for everything". Explain it with the finance report, the shop dashboard and the fraud backfill, and say what stops three engines from meaning three copies of the data.
explain_back.answer: We sized each piece of work by what it reads, not by the 4 TB table. The finance report reads 4 of 60 columns for 30 of 1,095 days: about 7 GB. One machine scans that in a few seconds, and its working set is tiny, so DuckDB on one machine answers it with no cluster to run; Spark would spend more time scheduling than reading. The shop dashboard reads about 22 GB per query, but 40 people open it at once with a 30-second budget. One cloud machine reading object storage at 1.5 GB/s would need almost 10 minutes for all of them. That needs about 20 machines working in parallel and answering in seconds, which is what Trino is for. The fraud backfill reads 2 TB and joins three years of history. Its scan would fit a two-hour window on one machine, but the join needs about 600 GB of memory at once, and the job runs for an hour. So it needs a cluster that spreads the state and retries failed tasks: Spark. All three read the same Iceberg tables through one REST catalog, so there's one copy of the data and one set of access rules, and each piece of work can move to another engine later if its numbers change.

deeper.body:
The method leaves out three things that matter in practice. Cost: a cluster that sits idle between nightly jobs costs money, while serverless engines (ones you don't run yourself, billed per use) charge per byte scanned, which rewards exactly the skipping this track taught. Operations: every engine is something to upgrade, watch and secure, so a small team should count engines the way it counts libraries it depends on. And many writers: the catalog's compare-and-swap (Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs) lets several engines write the same table, but frequent writers that clash, such as a streaming load and a compaction job on the same partitions, still need a schedule.

DuckDB keeps growing toward shared use. DuckDB 2.0 added Quack, a client-server protocol: one DuckDB process can serve others over the network (`-serve` and `-connect` in the command-line tool, `CONNECT` in SQL), so a small team can share one warm database instead of each analyst loading the data. MotherDuck runs DuckDB as a cloud service, and DuckLake (Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs) gives DuckDB a table format for many users.

Spark is moving the other way, toward fast small queries. Besides single-task execution in 4.3, projects such as Apache Gluten (with Velox) and Apache DataFusion Comet plug native C++ or Rust code that works on whole vectors into Spark's plans, and Databricks runs its own native engine, Photon. The gap measured in this lesson is mostly fixed cost per query and row-by-row JVM work, and both are under attack.

For orchestration, Airflow 3 also versions DAGs (a run finishes on the version it started with) and can start runs on outside events, not only on time and assets. A team that already runs a general workflow tool for its own programs can use it for data jobs too; Airflow's advantage is its large set of ready-made operators for Spark, Trino, dbt and the clouds.
